title: The Girl Who Planted a Door
summary: Iara finds a seed that promises to return anything lost — including the brother she hasn't seen in a year. But what grows from a seed like that is never exactly what was planted.

chapters.title: The Seed No One Planted
chapters.body:
After Iara's brother went away, the house grew too big. Not that she had grown — it was that silence takes up so much room. Bento had been the kind of boy who filled the rooms with noise: whistling, slamming doors, laughter too loud for a small house. For a year now he hadn't come home, and no one in the house would say where he'd gone or when he'd be back. The grown-ups got teary-eyed when she asked, so she stopped asking. She learned that some absences you carry in silence.

Iara took to sleeping with her brother's old coat, which still faintly smelled of him — of woods, of rain, of boy. Every night she hugged that smell, and every day it was a little fainter, and she knew that when the smell ran out, it would be like losing Bento a second time.

It was on one of those nights, rummaging through the coat's pockets for more of the smell, that she found the seed.

It was the size of an olive, dark, hard, with golden veins that seemed to move when she wasn't looking straight at them. It didn't look like a seed of anything she knew. And there was something carved into it, tiny letters in a spiral, which Iara brought close to the candle to read:

Plant what you lost. Harvest what returned. Beware the difference.

Iara was no fool. She knew that things that promise too much usually charge dearly. But she was eleven years old with a brother-shaped hole in her chest, and when you have a hole like that, the part of you that knows to be careful speaks softly and the part that wants to fill the hole shouts.

In the yard, under the moon, she dug a small hole with her own hands. She laid the seed in it. She thought of Bento with all her might — the whistle, the laugh, the way he called her "Ant" because she was small and stubborn. She covered the seed with earth. She watered it with water and with two or three tears that fell without asking permission.

"Come back," she whispered. "Please, come back."

The next morning, there was a sprout.

Not an ordinary green sprout. It was pale, almost white, and it grew too fast — you could see, if you stayed very still, the millimeters appearing. By noon it was a shrub. By nightfall, a tree as tall as she was, with dark bark and leaves shaped like hands. And in the trunk, about where a heart would be if trees had hearts, a vertical crack had begun to form, smooth and dark, with a wooden handle growing out of it like a branch.

A door was growing.

Iara should have been afraid. Part of her was. But the other part, the part with the hole, laid her hand on the warm bark of the tree and felt, on the other side of the growing door, something impossible and wonderful: the distant, muffled sound of a whistle. Bento's whistle.

"You came back," she said to the tree, and laughed and cried at the same time.

From inside the house, her mother called her to dinner. Iara looked at the door still half-formed in the trunk, at the handle still soft as a sprout, and decided to wait until the next morning, when she'd be ready. She promised the tree she would come back.

But that night, lying with the coat that already barely smelled of anything, Iara couldn't sleep. Because the more she thought about the whistle she'd heard, the more she noticed something the careful part of her had been trying to say quietly all day:

The whistle was right. The melody was Bento's. But he whistled it backward. Like a tape played in reverse. Like a memory someone had copied without quite understanding what they were copying.

chapters.title: The Brother Inside
chapters.body:
In the morning, the door was finished.

The tree had stopped growing at the height of the roof, and the crack in the trunk was now a whole door, of dark wood, with a handle worn smooth by much — or by no — use. On the other side, the whistle went on, quietly, backward. Iara stood before it a long while, her hand on the cold handle, listening to the careful part and the part with the hole quarrel inside her chest.

Plant what you lost. Harvest what returned. Beware the difference.

The difference. She turned the handle.

Inside the tree there was no wood, no trunk, no root. There was a forest — but a wrong forest, like a drawing of a forest made by someone who had only heard it described. The trees were too tall and too thin, without bark, white as bone. There was no sky, only a grey brightness that came from everywhere and from nowhere. And the ground was soft and dark and breathed slowly, rising and falling, as if the whole forest lay upon something enormous and asleep.

And there, in a clearing, was Bento.

Iara's heart leapt — and then hesitated. Because it was Bento, yes. The hair, the height, the coat exactly like the one she hugged every night. But he stood with his back to her, very still, and whistled the melody backward, and when Iara called his name, he took too long to turn. And when he turned, his face was right in every detail and wrong as a whole, the way a reflection in still water is you but isn't. His eyes were kind. Too kind. They smiled before the rest of his face, as if reading instructions.

"Ant," he said. "You came."

The right word. The right nickname. And still Iara felt a chill, because Bento never said "Ant" like that, with that dripping sweetness. Bento said "Ant" laughing, half-teasing, in a brother's way. This thing said it the way someone offers candy through a car window.

"You're not Bento," said Iara, and her voice trembled, because part of her wanted so, so badly to be wrong.

The thing with her brother's face tilted its head. The smile did not move.

"I am what you planted," it said. "You planted longing. Longing is a strange seed. It doesn't return the person. It grows a new person around the hole the person left. I am made of the shape of your brother's absence. I fit perfectly." It took a step forward, and the ground breathed beneath its feet. "Stay with me here, Ant. Here the longing doesn't hurt. Here I'll never go away again. You only have to close the door from the inside."

And Iara, who had carried that absence in silence for a whole year, felt the temptation like a current pulling at her ankles. To stay. To never feel the hole again. To have a brother who would never leave, even if he was a false brother, a brother the shape of the absence.

But then she looked again at the too-kind eyes, and thought of something the careful part had been trying to say from the start, and that now, at last, spoke loud enough for her to hear: the real Bento would never want me trapped in a forest of bone to escape missing him. The real Bento would want me to live.

The longing was not the problem. The longing was the price of having loved someone. And this being — this false brother — was not offering her Bento. It was offering her to forget that Bento had been real.

"No," said Iara. "I didn't plant you to stop missing him." Her voice steadied. "I'd rather have the real longing than a lie that doesn't hurt."

The thing's smile, at last, slid off its face. And the whole forest, beneath her feet, opened its eyes.

chapters.title: What Is Harvested
chapters.body:
The breathing ground rose up.

What Iara had taken for soil was the thing — the whole forest was a single vast being, and the white trees were its fingers, and the clearing was the palm of its hand, and she stood right in the middle of it. The false brother dissolved into the air like smoke, having been only the bait, the sweet little face the thing used to call sad children into itself. Because that was what it fed on: children with a hole in the chest, willing to trade real pain for a false comfort.

The finger-trees curled to close over Iara.

She ran. The door — the dark wooden door in the trunk she had come through — still stood open back there, a rectangle of real morning light in the midst of that grey, dead brightness. Iara ran for it with everything she had, and the hand-ground tilted to spill her back toward the center, and the finger-trees swept the air behind her, cold as the gap between things.

A finger-tree closed in front of the door, barring the way.

Iara stopped, out of breath. The door was right there, on the other side of that branch, white and smooth as bone. And she understood, with the sudden clarity of someone too afraid to fool herself, that she wasn't going to make it through by running. The thing was too big. But she remembered the words on the seed — harvest what returned — and remembered that a door that grows from a seed of longing has a root. And every root can be cut by the one who planted it.

She had not planted a tree. She had planted a door. And the door obeyed her, not the thing, because it was her longing, Iara's own, that had made it grow.

"Close," Iara ordered, with all the authority a heartbroken eleven-year-old can muster. "You grew from me. So you obey me. Close!"

The door shuddered in the distant trunk. The thing felt what was coming and howled — a mouthless sound, made of wind in dry branches — and hurled all its finger-trees at once to seize Iara before she could give the final command.

"Close with me on the outside," Iara shouted, "and you on the inside. Forever!"

And she jumped. Not away from the thing — under the finger-tree that barred the door, rolling across the breathing ground, scraping her knees, sliding just beneath the white branch at the very instant the door, obeying the girl who had planted it, began to close.

Iara crossed the threshold and fell onto the wet grass of her own yard, in the real morning, with the real sun and the real smell of earth. Behind her, inside the trunk, the thing stretched a single white finger through the gap — and the door closed on it with a dull, final thud. The finger, severed, fell onto the grass, turned to smoke, turned to nothing.

The whole tree groaned. The dark bark wrinkled, dried, and in a few seconds the entire tree collapsed in on itself, shrinking, withering, until nothing was left but a hole in the earth and, at the bottom of it, the seed — dark and hard again, its golden veins still, waiting for the next sad child.

Iara picked up the seed. She did not plant it. She did not throw it away, either, because things like that have a way of coming back. She kept it in a glass jar, on a high shelf, where she could keep watch over it.

Then she went inside. Her mother was in the kitchen, teary-eyed as she always got when the subject circled Bento. Iara came close and, for the first time in a year, spoke her brother's name aloud — not to bring him back, but because names spoken with love are the right way to carry those who are gone.

"Tell me about Bento," she asked. "A real story."

And her mother, surprised, cried — but this time smiling — and told her.
